newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel drafts tax bill to calm opposition critics.
newsitem.headline: Waigel drafts tax bill to calm opposition critics.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Tuesday presented a draft tax reform bill that would bring forward 14 billion marks in planned tax cuts to 1998, countering opposition criticism with concrete proposals.
The bill means Chancellor Helmut Kohl will have a plan in hand when he meets Social Democrat leader Oskar Lafontaine to discuss tax reform next Monday.

Despite pressures to consolidate government finances to qualify for European monetary union (EMU) starting in 1999, Germany has decided it must cut taxes and simplify the tax system to stimulate corporate investment and create jobs.
Coalition leaders also decided against a government spending freeze for the time being, buying additional leverage against the SPD.
While lowering tax rates, mainly for corporations, the Waigel draft would also close some tax breaks, so the net drain on federal coffers would be about six billion marks next year.

The bill, which Waigel presented to the cabinet for comment, is the result of a comprehensive two-stage tax reform plan agreed by coalition leaders to cut a total of 30 billion marks in taxes by 1999.

The SPD, which would have to approve parts of the tax reform bill if it is to gain the necessary majority to go ahead, ideally wants a changed version of the original tax reform plan to be implemented in full next year.
But last week it called the partial acceleration a step in the right direction.
The centrepiece of Waigel's bill is a two percentage point reduction in the unpopular solidarity surcharge on income taxes.

While cutting corporate tax rates, the bill would also eliminate seven billion marks in tax benefits for corporations, particularly for additions to reserves. The government would have to fund about six billion marks in tax cuts through parallel reductions in spending.

Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said he hoped parliament would approve the bill before its summer break. A draft bill for the remainder of the planned tax reform will be ready next month, he said.
The government will talk with the SPD about bringing further pieces of the 1999 package ahead one year if financing can be secured, Hausmann said.
The government hopes for SPD concessions in cutting outlays for asylum seekers and welfare recipients. Bonn also sees a need to cut government consumption to increase investment.
The coalition's parliamentary manager, Joachim Hoerster, said a spending freeze was undesirable because it would hit government investment much harder than consumption.

The Berliner Zeitung, citing coalition sources, said the government would have to cut up to 20 billion marks in subsidies and social spending if it is to keep its deficit below three percent of gross domestic product, as required to qualify for EMU.

The tax reform plan reached by a Waigel-led commission in January called for corporate taxes to be cut next year to 40 percent from 45 percent, and taxes on dividends to be cut to 28 percent from 30 percent.
The new plan would reduce state government revenues by 1.3 billion marks and local government revenues by 168 million marks next year, but it would raise income in years following.
Joachim Poss, the SPD's parliamentary fiscal policy spokesman, said the delays in increased state and local revenues rendered the Waigel plan irresponsible.
